data.cause: The primary resolver on dns1.lan rate-limits the whole client subnet (20 q/s per /24) and silently drops queries during brief traffic bursts; clients then fall back to gw.lan, whose unbound suppresses the forwarded .lan answers because they point into 10.0.0.0/8 (private-address filtering), so local names return ENOTFOUND until the burst passes — while internet names keep resolving via gw's DoT upstreams.
evidence: journalctl -u primary-dns on dns1.lan shows repeated 'ratelimit: 10.20.0.0/24 exceeded 20 q/s, dropping N queries' events (02:14, 09:41, 13:02), each followed within seconds by 'back under limit' — matching alerts a few times a day that clear within a minute or two

/opt/primary-dns/config.yaml sets ratelimit: 20 with ratelimit_subnet_len_ipv4: 24, i.e. one shared bucket for all of 10.20.0.0/24, and rewrites *.lan / nas.lan to 10.20.0.50 through the same limited path
mon.lan /etc/resolv.conf lists nameserver 10.20.0.3 first, then 10.20.0.1, so every lookup starts at the rate-limited resolver
dig @10.20.0.3 nas.lan normally returns NOERROR with A 10.20.0.50, confirming the rewrite itself is fine outside burst windows

drill nas.lan @127.0.0.1 on gw.lan returns NOERROR with ANSWER: 0 (empty) even though drill nas.lan @10.20.0.3 from the same host returns A 10.20.0.50 — the fallback resolver discards the private-address answer

/var/unbound/unbound.conf on gw.lan forwards lan. to 10.20.0.3 but also sets private-address: 10.0.0.0/8, so forwarded .lan answers pointing at 10.20.0.50 are filtered out; internet names forward to DoT upstreams and are unaffected
data.recommendation: Raise or remove the aggressive subnet rate limit on dns1's primary-dns (e.g., increase ratelimit far above normal LAN bursts, count per client rather than per /24, or exempt the locally rewritten *.lan data from limiting) so local-name queries are never dropped. Additionally, on gw.lan stop applying private-address suppression to answers forwarded for the lan. zone (e.g., serve the local .lan data as authoritative/local-zone there instead of forwarding), so the second DNS server can actually serve local names when dns1 is busy.
data.detail: primary resolver's aggressive rate limit silently drops LAN queries in bursts
